questions.q: What is the classical view of emotions that Barrett challenges?
a: Emotions are irrational reflexes, each tied to one brain region
Emotions are learned habits shaped by family life
Emotions are conscious choices made after careful thought
Emotions are physical sensations with no mental component
questions.why: Lesson 1 describes the classical view as treating emotions as inherited reflexes with a distinct brain area each.

questions.q: Why does Barrett reject the idea that each emotion has a distinct brain region?
a: The same brain areas are active during non-emotional thoughts too
Emotions happen too quickly for brain scans to capture
Only people with brain damage show clear emotional patterns
Different cultures use entirely different brain regions
questions.why: Lesson 1 says her scans showed the so-called emotion region also lighting up during ordinary perception and thought.

questions.q: What is the theory of constructed emotion?
a: The brain builds emotions from sensory input and past predictions
The brain releases a fixed set of emotions at birth
Emotions are copied from the expressions of caregivers
Emotions are produced by a single emotional center
questions.why: Lesson 2 says emotions are created on the spot by combining sensations with the brain's predictions from experience.

questions.q: Which example does the summary use to show culture shaping emotion concepts?
a: Tahitian has no word for sadness
Japanese has many words for embarrassment
German has a single word for joy
English lacks a word for contentment
questions.why: Lesson 3 says Tahitian uses a phrase about flu fatigue instead of a distinct word for sadness.

questions.q: What does the summary say about universal facial expressions of emotion?
a: They are a myth, since expressions vary by culture and situation
They prove that emotions are inborn and fixed
They are the same in every culture except for anger
They were only discovered in the last decade
questions.why: The overview and Lesson 1 say there is no universal facial expression for each emotion, such as smiling for joy.
